era.caption: Ἀθῆναι · {year}
era.note: still at peace: the war begins in the spring of 431, which the calendar never reaches, because spring returns to 432

summer.note: calm mornings; the meltemi rises in the afternoon; one rare storm

winter.note: mild rain; snow on the far mountains

look.light: brilliant and high-contrast, short blue shadows; marble the brightest thing on screen

stages.label: pressed from the store of olives
brought in by donkey from the burners on Parnes
stowed for the force at Potidaea

days_shown.label: Assembly day in November: ploughing and the olive harvest
January: the Lenaia, olives and the ship sheds

figures.note: on assembly days the assembly event takes him to the Pnyx
rides with the cavalry in the procession
at his bench (the role cobbler draws him)

parthenon.title: Παρθενών
parthenon.text: Begun in 447 and finished this year with its pediments, the Doric temple of 8 by 17 columns houses Pheidias's gold and ivory Athena. Its west pediment shows Athena and Poseidon contesting Attica; the frieze inside the colonnade shows a procession like the one you can follow today. Temples were painted, never plain white.

propylaia.title: Προπύλαια
propylaia.text: Mnesikles's gateway turns the steep west end of the rock into a stately climb: a central hall with Doric fronts, a ramp for the animals, a picture gallery in the north-west wing. This year the work stops; the lifting bosses stay on the blocks, and they are still there today.

nike_bastion.title: Πύργος
nike_bastion.text: A poros bastion beside the gateway with a small old shrine and altar of Athena Nike. The Ionic temple that stands here today is not built until the 420s.

approach.title: The approach
approach.text: A broad gravel ramp between retaining walls climbs from the Panathenaic Way to the gateway. Sacrificial cattle, riders and the whole procession come up this way.

old_temple.title: Ἀρχαῖος νεώς
old_temple.text: The temple burned by the Persians in 480. Whether its western rooms were repaired and used is debated; here its foundations lie open with a repaired, roofed west chamber where the old olive-wood Athena Polias may be kept.

pandroseion.title: Πανδρόσειον
pandroseion.text: A walled court round Athena's olive tree, her gift to the city in the contest with Poseidon. Burned in 480, it sprouted again the next day, people said. The tomb of the hero Kekrops lies beside it.

promachos.title: Ἀθηνᾶ Πρόμαχος
promachos.text: Pheidias's colossal bronze Athena, made around 460-450, stands between the gateway and the Old Temple. Sailors rounding Cape Sounion are said to have seen the glint of her spear tip. Her height is uncertain, perhaps 7 to 9 metres.

brauronion.title: Βραυρώνιον
brauronion.text: A sanctuary of Artemis of Brauron with a stoa of two wings, where women dedicated clothing to the goddess after childbirth, and girls served her as little bears.

chalkotheke.title: Χαλκοθήκη
chalkotheke.text: A plain hall where bronze dedications, weapons and votive offerings of Athena were stored, counted and listed on stone by her treasurers each year.

great_altar.title: Βωμός
great_altar.text: The altar where the procession ends. Cattle are sacrificed here, a hundred at the Great Panathenaia, and the meat is shared out to the people in the Kerameikos and the Agora.

zeus_polieus.title: Διὸς Πολιέως
zeus_polieus.text: The sanctuary of Zeus Polieus, where the old ox-sacrifice of the Dipolieia is held at midsummer: the axe is tried for the killing and thrown into the sea.

sculpt_yard.title: The sculptors' yard
sculpt_yard.text: Blocks with their bosses, roughed-out figures and a two-legged crane: the last of the pediment work is coming down. Citizens, metics and enslaved men cut stone here side by side. At dusk, some say, Pheidias still walks among the blocks.

hephaisteion.title: Ἡφαιστεῖον
hephaisteion.text: A Doric temple of 6 by 13 columns on Kolonos Agoraios, almost finished. Its metopes show Herakles and Theseus; its cult statues are not made until 421-415. Bronze casters work in pits on the hill around it.

royal_stoa.title: Στοὰ Βασίλειος
royal_stoa.text: A small Doric stoa facing the square where the king archon sits; the laws of Solon are displayed here on revolving wooden boards and on stone, for anyone to read.

stoa_zeus.title: Στοὰ τοῦ Διός
stoa_zeus.text: The Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios is dated around 430-420. In 432 it is at most a fresh building site, foundations pegged out, and possibly not begun at all; the game shows its footing.
stoa_zeus.epithet: Stoa of Zeus, a building site

old_bouleuterion.title: Βουλευτήριον
old_bouleuterion.text: The council of 500, fifty men from each tribe chosen by lot for a year, meets here to prepare the assembly's business.

tholos.title: Θόλος
tholos.text: The fifty councillors on duty, the prytaneis, eat here at public expense, and a third of them sleep here, so the city is never without a government.

stoa_poikile.title: Στοὰ Ποικίλη
stoa_poikile.text: A long colonnade facing the Agora, hung with great painted panels of Marathon, the Amazons, the fall of Troy and Oinoe. Anyone may walk and talk here. The captured Spartan shields Pausanias saw came later, from 425 and 421.

twelve_gods.title: Βωμὸς τῶν δώδεκα θεῶν
twelve_gods.text: A fenced altar and a place of refuge for suppliants; distances from Athens were measured from here, the city's milestone point.

tyrannicides.title: Harmodios and Aristogeiton
tyrannicides.text: The bronze group by Kritios and Nesiotes (477/6) honours the two men who killed the tyrant's brother in 514. When the Persians carried off the first statue, the city simply made a new one.

se_fountain.title: Κρήνη
se_fountain.text: Water runs from lion-head spouts into the basin; women and enslaved girls fill their hydriai here at dawn and in the evening.

lawcourt.title: Δικαστήριον
lawcourt.text: A walled enclosure probably used by the courts (the identification is debated). Juries of hundreds of citizens over thirty are paid two obols a day.

horos.title: Ὅρος
horos.text: "I am the boundary of the Agora", says the inscribed marble post. Beyond it, people under a curse may not pass.

simon_shop.title: Σίμων
simon_shop.text: A shoemaker's house and shop at the Agora's edge, where hobnails and a cup inscribed SIMONOS were found. Socrates is said to have sat at his bench.

eleusinion.title: Ἐλευσίνιον
eleusinion.text: The city sanctuary of Demeter and Kore on the Panathenaic Way, linked by the Sacred Way to Eleusis and its Mysteries.

dipylon.title: Δίπυλον
dipylon.text: The largest gate of Athens: two gate towers and a deep court. The Panathenaic Way begins here, and the procession sets out at dawn.

sacred_gate.title: Ἱερὰ Πύλη
sacred_gate.text: The Sacred Way to Eleusis leaves through this gate, with the Eridanos flowing in its channel beside the road.

pnyx.title: Πνύξ
pnyx.text: Every adult male citizen may come here to speak and vote by a show of hands. The audience sits on the natural slope facing the speakers' platform; perhaps forty meetings a year.

meton_dial.title: Ἡλιοτρόπιον
meton_dial.text: Here the astronomer Meton observed the summer solstice of 432 BC and proposed a cycle of 19 years that brings the moon's months back into step with the sun's year.

theatre.title: Θέατρον Διονύσου
theatre.text: Wooden bleachers on the south slope face a round earth orchestra with an altar and a simple wooden stage. The stone theatre comes a century later. Next spring Euripides will stage the Medea here.

dionysos_temple.title: Ναὸς Διονύσου
dionysos_temple.text: A small poros temple of Dionysos Eleuthereus beside the theatre, home of the old wooden image of the god that is carried in at the City Dionysia.

odeion.title: Ὠιδεῖον
odeion.text: A square hall with a forest of columns under a pyramidal roof; Plutarch says it imitated the Persian king's tent. The music contests of the Great Panathenaia are held here.

olympieion.title: Ὀλυμπιεῖον
olympieion.text: A huge platform begun by the tyrants in the 6th century and abandoned; column drums lie in the grass. It will not be finished for six hundred years.

kallirrhoe.title: Καλλιρρόη
kallirrhoe.text: A spring in the bed of the Ilissos whose water was used for bridal baths. Plane trees and a grassy bank make it a place to sit and talk in the heat.

lyceum.title: Λύκειον
lyceum.text: A gymnasium in a grove outside the walls with a running track and a shrine of Apollo Lykeios. Hoplites and cavalry drill here; athletes run and wrestle in the afternoon.

shipsheds.title: Νεώσοικοι
shipsheds.text: Long rows of roofed slipways where the triremes are hauled out of the water to dry. Athens has some 300 warships in 431.

harbour.title: Κάνθαρος
harbour.text: The great harbour of Piraeus: quays, the long stoas of the emporion where merchants deal in grain from the Black Sea and Egypt, moles with towers narrowing the mouth.

pentelikon_quarry.title: Πεντελικόν
pentelikon_quarry.text: Bright white-gold faces cut in steps, wedge slots, a sledge ramp: the Parthenon's marble starts here and goes down to the city on sledges and ox carts.

pericles.title: Περικλῆς
pericles.text: Elected general year after year, Pericles persuaded the Athenians to rebuild the Acropolis with the allies' tribute. Thucydides wrote that Athens was in name a democracy but in fact ruled by its first man. This summer, Sparta's patience is running out.

aspasia.title: Ἀσπασία
aspasia.text: A foreign woman of learning and wit, Pericles's partner. Socrates is said to have learned rhetoric from her. Comic poets mocked her; later writers admired her. As a metic, her son by Pericles needed a special vote to become a citizen.

socrates.title: Σωκράτης
socrates.text: A stonemason's son, aged about 37, who walks barefoot in all weather and asks people what courage, justice or beauty really are, until they admit they do not know. He wrote nothing. Soon he will march to Potidaea as a hoplite.

sophocles.title: Σοφοκλῆς
sophocles.text: Winner of more drama contests than anyone, and general with Pericles in the war against Samos. He also serves as priest of a healing hero. His Antigone asks what a citizen owes to the city and what to the gods.

euripides.title: Εὐριπίδης
euripides.text: Restless, questioning, fond of books; tradition says he liked solitude. Next spring he will stage the Medea, a woman's fury against the man who betrayed her. It will come third. This afternoon he watches its chorus rehearse, a scroll in his lap.

pheidias.title: Φειδίας
pheidias.text: He made the gold and ivory Athena inside the Parthenon and directed its sculpture. Enemies of Pericles accused him of stealing the statue's gold. One ancient writer says he died in an Athenian prison; another that he left for Olympia, where his Zeus became a wonder of the world. This summer, his yard works on without him.

mnesikles.title: Μνησικλῆς
mnesikles.text: His gateway to the Acropolis turns a steep rock into a stately climb. This year the work stops, with the stone bosses for lifting still on the blocks; the money and the men are wanted elsewhere. The bosses are still there today.

protagoras.title: Πρωταγόρας
protagoras.text: 'Man is the measure of all things.' The famous teacher from Abdera charges fees to train young men in argument, and walks with a crowd of pupils who turn about as he turns. Plato imagined Socrates debating him at the house of Kallias.

meton.title: Μέτων
meton.text: On the Pnyx this summer he marked the solstice, and he proposes a cycle of 19 years that brings the moon's months back into step with the sun's year. Comic poets laughed at him; astronomers used his cycle for centuries.

alcibiades.title: Ἀλκιβιάδης
alcibiades.text: Eighteen, rich, beautiful and reckless, and adored by the city; today he rides with the cavalry in the procession, long-haired, in a purple cloak. At Potidaea, Socrates will save his life. Later he will betray Athens and return to it, twice.

solon.title: Σόλων
solon.text: Long ago he freed Athenians enslaved for debt and wrote the laws still kept on revolving wooden boards in the Royal Stoa. He wrote poems, too: 'I grow old, always learning many things.' At dusk he is remembered before the stoa.

themistocles.title: Θεμιστοκλῆς
themistocles.text: He persuaded Athens to spend its silver on ships, won at Salamis and walled Piraeus. Ostracised, he ended his life as a Persian governor. At dusk he is remembered on the quay, looking toward Salamis. His harbour still hums below him.
themistocles.epithet: Themistocles, founder of the fleet (a memory)

theseus.title: Θησεύς
theseus.text: Slayer of the Minotaur, he joined the villages of Attica into a single city, the Athenians said. Kimon found his bones on Skyros and brought them home in triumph. In the procession a young man walks in his likeness, club in hand.

rhapsode.title: The rhapsode
rhapsode.text: Every fourth summer, at the Great Panathenaia, singers recite the Iliad and Odyssey in turn, by law. This year is not a great year, but he sings anyway. Listen, and Achilles' anger and Odysseus' long road home rise in the dusk.

athena.title: Ἀθηνᾶ
athena.text: She won Attica from Poseidon by giving the olive. The Athenians bring her old olive-wood statue a new woven robe, perhaps every summer, certainly every fourth. The gold and ivory Athena in the Parthenon was a treasure as much as an image.

poseidon.title: Ποσειδῶν
poseidon.text: He struck the rock with his trident and a salt spring rose, but the gods gave the land to Athena. Athenians still showed the marks in the rock, and honoured him beside the hero Erechtheus. Sailors and rowers still pray to him before they put out.

herakles.title: Ἡρακλῆς
herakles.text: Strongest of heroes, son of Zeus and a mortal woman. His labours fill the metopes of the Hephaisteion and the Athenian treasury at Delphi; the Athenians claimed they were the first to honour him as a god. Look for his lion skin and club.

philinna.title: Philinna
philinna.text: Philinna spins wool before sunrise and weaves until noon. Her husband sits on the Council this year. She goes out for water, for festivals and to visit her sister. Her daughter will carry a basket in next year's procession, if the priestesses choose her.

mania.title: Mania
mania.text: Mania was born in Phrygia and sold at Ephesus as a girl. She has raised two of Philinna's children. Athenian grave stones sometimes honour nurses like her by name, kindly. She hums Phrygian songs to the baby, in a language no one else in the house knows.

manes.title: Manes
manes.text: Manes knows the kiln's moods: three firings, air in, air out, then in again, and red clay turns black where the painter's slip lies. He has saved some coins; some enslaved craftsmen in Athens worked on their own and paid their master a share.

kephalos.title: Kephalos
kephalos.text: Kephalos came from Syracuse at Pericles's invitation and makes shields in Piraeus in a large workshop. Metics like him pay a special tax, serve in the army and cannot own land, but Athens could not run without them. His sons will keep the workshop going.

sosias.title: Sosias
sosias.text: Sosias walks from Acharnai with two donkeys of oak charcoal. He votes in the assembly when the harvest allows, and grumbles that the city folk talk too much. His charcoal feeds the potters' kilns and the smithies, and warms the city's winters.

nikarete.title: Nikarete
nikarete.text: Nikarete sells barley cakes and wheat loaves from a basket in the Agora. Bread-women had a reputation for sharp tongues. She has seen every general of the last thirty years buy her bread, and tells you so, twice, before you have paid.

toxamis.title: Toxamis
toxamis.text: Toxamis is one of the city's Scythian archers: public slaves who keep order in the assembly and the courts. On assembly mornings they sweep the Agora with a rope dyed red, and, ancient commentators said, anyone marked with the red loses their pay.

euphiletos.title: Euphiletos
euphiletos.text: Euphiletos tends olives and vines outside the walls and brings his oil to the city. In a war he would serve as a hoplite. Tonight he will sleep in the city, at his cousin's in Kollytos, to see the procession at dawn.

hegeso.title: Hegeso
hegeso.text: Hegeso is eleven. Girls her age weave the new robe for Athena with the priestesses, and a few of good family carry baskets in the procession. She practises walking with a basket on her head, very straight, and does not drop it once.

simon.title: Simon
simon.text: Simon makes sandals at the corner of the Agora. Ancient writers said Socrates often sat at his bench to talk with young men too young to enter the Agora. The hobnails and his cup were found by archaeologists, just outside the boundary stone.

democracy.title: Democracy
democracy.text: In 432, a few tens of thousands of men governed themselves directly: they spoke and voted in the assembly, sat on the Council by lot and judged in huge juries. Women, slaves and foreigners could not vote; Athens's freedom rested partly on the tribute of others.

philosophy.title: Philosophy
philosophy.text: Earlier thinkers asked what the world is made of. In Athens, sophists like Protagoras taught argument for fees, and Socrates asked everyone what justice, courage and the good life really are. The questions moved from the stars to the street.
philosophy.epithet: From nature to how to live

drama.title: Tragedy and comedy
drama.text: Plays are staged for Dionysos at the City Dionysia in spring and the Lenaia in winter, with choruses of citizens, three actors in masks and a prize for the best poet. A rich citizen pays for each chorus. The seats are still wooden.

history.title: History
history.text: Herodotus, tradition says, read from his Histories of the Persian Wars in Athens. A young Athenian named Thucydides is about to begin a history of the war that is coming, written to be a possession for all time, and to tell what really happened.

curves.title: The Parthenon's curves
curves.text: Nothing in the Parthenon is quite straight. The base rises about 6 cm in the middle of the short ends and about 10-11 cm along the long sides; the columns lean slightly inward and swell a little. Why the builders did it, to correct the eye or for life and tension, is still argued.

planning.title: A city on a grid
planning.text: Hippodamos of Miletus laid out Piraeus in a regular grid of streets, with zones for the harbour, the market and the houses, and argued about the best way to order a city. Athens itself, older, grew in winding lanes around its rock.

medicine.title: Hippocratic medicine
medicine.text: Physicians of the Hippocratic school watched symptoms, took notes and looked for natural causes rather than divine ones. Athens hired public physicians. The cult of the healing god Asklepios arrives only in 420, and the great plague, which no physician can stop, in 430.

laurion.title: The silver of Laurion
laurion.text: The owls in every purse come from the state mines at Laurion in south Attica, worked mostly by enslaved men in narrow, airless galleries. The mines are off this map; their silver is everywhere on it, in every purse and on every stall.

league.title: The League and its tribute
league.text: Founded against Persia in 478, the Delian League is now an Athenian empire of some 150 cities. Their tribute arrives by sea; a sixtieth goes to Athena and is listed on stone on the Acropolis. Chios and Lesbos still send ships instead.

megara.title: The Megarian decree
megara.text: This year Athens has shut the traders of Megara out of the Agora and the League's harbours. A Megarian at the boundary stone is turned back. Sparta will call it one cause of the war that begins next spring, together with Potidaea.

potidaea.title: Potidaea
potidaea.text: Potidaea, a city of the League in the north, has revolted with Corinth's help. Hoplites march down between the Long Walls to the ships; Socrates and Alcibiades will be among them. The great war with Sparta is only months away.

metics.title: Metics
metics.text: Perhaps ten to twenty-five thousand free foreigners live in Attica with their families: traders, bankers, potters, shield-makers. They pay a special tax, serve in the army and the fleet and carry trays in the procession, but cannot vote or own land.

slavery.title: Enslaved Athenians
slavery.text: A very large number of the people you see are enslaved: nurses, porters, kiln-men, miners, even the city's own archers. Many work beside free men at the same tasks; some live on their own and pay their owner a share. Their freedom was not theirs to choose.

women.title: Women's lives
women.text: Citizen women run the household, spin and weave, fetch water, visit, mourn and serve as priestesses; wealthy women go out less. Poorer women sell in the market and nurse. Women could not vote, but the city's greatest festivals needed them.

symposium.title: The symposium
symposium.text: After dinner, men recline on couches in the andron, mix wine with water in a krater, sing, play kottabos and talk. Hired musicians, often enslaved, play the aulos. From the street you hear only laughter and a lyre, late into the night.

burial.title: Funerals
burial.text: The dead are carried out before dawn, as an old law requires, with women singing laments and an aulos player, to graves along the roads outside the walls. Painted stelai and white-ground oil flasks honour them, and families come back to the graves with ribbons and oil.

seller.title: Market seller
seller.text: Sells from a trestle stall: bread, oil, pots, fish, garlic; bargains loudly and packs up at midday.

banker.title: Money-changer
banker.text: At his table he tests coins, weighs them and changes foreign silver for Athenian owls.

citizen.title: Citizen
citizen.text: In a himation, he shops in the morning, talks in the stoas and walks the city in the cool of the evening.

elder.title: Old man
elder.text: Sits in the shade of the stoa with his staff and watches the city go by, ready to argue.

porter.title: Porter
porter.text: Enslaved or free, he carries sacks and jars between the quays, the gates and the stalls.

scythian.title: Scythian archer
scythian.text: A public slave of the city in a pointed cap and trousers, keeping order in the Agora and the courts.

water_carrier.title: Water carrier
water_carrier.text: Fills her hydria at the fountain house, lifts it onto her head and walks home.

philosopher.title: A talker
philosopher.text: Walks in the stoa with whoever will listen and asks what they mean by what they say.

youth.title: Young man
youth.text: In a short cloak and broad hat, he follows a teacher about the Agora and argues back.

councillor.title: Councillor
councillor.text: Chosen by lot for a year, he prepares the assembly's business and dines in the Tholos when his tribe is on duty.

herald.title: Herald
herald.text: Calls the citizens to order, proclaims decrees and calls for silence before a speech.

juror.title: Juror
juror.text: A citizen over thirty with a bronze ticket, paid two obols a day to judge a case before sunset.

potter.title: Potter
potter.text: Wedges the clay, throws a pot on the kick wheel, trims it and fixes the handles.

painter.title: Vase painter
painter.text: Draws the figures in fine slip, fills the ground black around them and adds the details before the firing.

kiln_man.title: Kiln-man
kiln_man.text: Stacks the kiln, stokes it and controls the air through three firings.

clay_digger.title: Clay digger
clay_digger.text: Digs clay in the pits outside the Dipylon and carries it to the workshops to soak.

mourner.title: Mourner
mourner.text: Brings oil flasks and ribbons to a family grave and sits awhile beside the painted stone.

priest.title: Priest or priestess
priest.text: Opens the shrine, pours a libation, prays and tends the sacred olive.

woman.title: Citizen woman
woman.text: A himation drawn over her hair, she fetches water, visits a neighbour and stops at the household shrine.

mason.title: Mason
mason.text: Hoists and sets blocks, clamps them with iron and lead and dresses the faces.

sculptor.title: Sculptor
sculptor.text: Roughs out with the point, works with the claw chisel, smooths with a rasp and emery.

owl.title: Little owl
owl.text: Athena's bird, common on the rock and the walls; it calls at night.

enslaved_woman.title: Enslaved woman
enslaved_woman.text: A nurse or a maid, carrying water, a baby or the shopping through the lanes.

shopkeeper.title: Shopkeeper
shopkeeper.text: Sells from the front room of her house: wool, garlands, perfume, lamps.

weaver.title: Wool-worker
weaver.text: Cards, spins and weaves on the warp-weighted loom, as women of every class did.

enslaved_man.title: Enslaved worker
enslaved_man.text: Carries firewood and water, works in a shop or a field, often beside his owner.

child.title: Child
child.text: Plays knucklebones, spins a top or chases a hoop in the lanes.

school.title: Schoolboy
school.text: Learns his letters, Homer and the lyre at a small school in Melite.

paidagogos.title: Paidagogos
paidagogos.text: The enslaved man who walks a boy to school and keeps an eye on him.

smith.title: Smith
smith.text: Works the bellows and hammers bronze and iron into tools, armour and shield facings.

caster.title: Bronze caster
caster.text: Packs moulds, melts bronze and pours it in pits on the hill of the Hephaisteion.

chorus.title: Chorus member
chorus.text: A citizen who rehearses the songs and steps of a tragic chorus for months.

aulos.title: Aulos player
aulos.text: Plays the double pipes for the chorus by day and at a symposium by night.

rower.title: Rower
rower.text: A poorer citizen, metic or enslaved man who pulls an oar in a trireme, in time to the piper.

docker.title: Dock worker
docker.text: Hauls ropes and carries amphorae and sacks between the ships and the emporion.

metic.title: Merchant
metic.text: A resident foreigner trading grain, wine and timber in the emporion of Piraeus.

shipwright.title: Shipwright
shipwright.text: Shapes pine and fir from Macedon with the adze and pitches the hulls of triremes.

ionian.title: Ionian visitor
ionian.text: A trader or envoy from the League's Greek cities across the Aegean.

thracian.title: Thracian
thracian.text: From the north, where Athens gets timber and silver, and many of its slaves.

spectator.title: Festival-goer
spectator.text: Out for the Panathenaia in a clean himation, to watch the procession pass and claim a share of the meat.

farmer.title: Farmer
farmer.text: Hoes the vines and olives, brings the threshed barley home and goes to the city on market days.

thresher.title: Thresher
thresher.text: Spreads the barley on the floor, drives the animals round and winnows the grain in the wind.

presser.title: Olive presser
presser.text: Crushes olives from the store, packs the baskets under the beam and decants the oil into jars.

herder.title: Goatherd
herder.text: Takes the goats and sheep up the hills at dawn and brings them down at dusk.

athlete.title: Athlete
athlete.text: Runs, wrestles and scrapes the oil and dust off with a strigil, naked as Greeks trained.

hoplite.title: Hoplite
hoplite.text: A citizen who can afford a bronze shield, helmet and spear, drilling at the Lyceum.

trainer.title: Trainer
trainer.text: Watches the athletes with his rod, corrects a hold and calls the pace.

quarry_hauler.title: Quarry hauler
quarry_hauler.text: Free and enslaved men rope the blocks down the sledge ramp and clear the spoil.

quarryman.title: Quarryman
quarryman.text: Cuts a channel round a block, drives the wedges and levers the marble free.

ploughman.title: Ploughman
ploughman.text: When the cranes call overhead, says Hesiod, it is time to plough: the farmer yokes his oxen and sows barley and wheat in the soft ground.

reaper.title: Reaper
reaper.text: Attic barley ripens early: reapers cut it with sickles in May and wheat in June, and carry the sheaves to the threshing floor.

olive_picker.title: Olive picker
olive_picker.text: Olives are beaten from the branches with sticks or picked by hand onto cloths, then carried to the press for the winter's oil.

vintager.title: Grape picker
vintager.text: In September the grapes are cut and trodden in the vat; the new wine rests in jars until the Anthesteria opens it.

pruner.title: Pruner
pruner.text: Hesiod's farmer prunes his vines before the swallow comes back, in the last cold weeks of winter.

shearer.title: Shearer
shearer.text: Sheep are shorn in spring before the heat; the wool goes to the women's looms for the year's cloth.

thesmophoria.title: Thesmophoria
thesmophoria.text: Citizen women keep Demeter's festival for three days on the hill of the Thesmophorion. Men may not attend, and what is done there is theirs to know.

lenaia.title: Lenaia
lenaia.text: A winter festival of Dionysus with contests in comedy and tragedy, held when no foreigners are in the city, as Aristophanes later jokes.

anthesteria.title: Anthesteria
anthesteria.text: In early spring the jars of last autumn's wine are opened. Children of three get their first little jug, and the dead are thought to walk the streets for a day.

ship_sheds.title: Ship sheds
ship_sheds.text: Through the closed season the triremes rest in their long sheds at Zea and Mounychia, and shipwrights repair hulls, oars and tackle for the spring.

strings.first_visit: Hekatombaion, 432 BC. The Parthenon is finished, the Propylaia has just stopped, and at dawn the procession leaves the Dipylon for the rock.
strings.procession: The Panathenaic procession has left the Dipylon.
strings.assembly: The archers sweep the Agora with the red rope: the assembly meets on the Pnyx.
strings.embark: Hoplites march down between the Long Walls to the ships for Potidaea.
strings.torch_race: Torches in the dark: the runners race from the Academy to the rock.
strings.wedding: Torches and an aulos: a bride is led to her new home.
strings.decorate_zone: A courtyard house in Melite, with a garden to furnish.
strings.thargelia: Thargelia: the first fruits are carried to Apollo.
strings.skira: Skira: the priestess walks out under a white parasol.
strings.oschophoria: Youths carry vine branches heavy with grapes down to Phaleron.
strings.thesmophoria: The women go up to the Thesmophorion: no men today.
strings.rural_dionysia: In the demes the Rural Dionysia: a procession, songs and jokes.
strings.lenaia: The Lenaia: comedies in the theatre, for Athenians only.
strings.anthesteria: The Anthesteria: the new wine is opened; children carry little jugs.
strings.vintage: Grapes are trodden in the vats.
strings.ship_sheds: The triremes are in their sheds; the shipwrights are at work.
strings.braziers: Braziers are lit in the shops against the cold.
strings.flurry: A few snowflakes over the Agora. They do not settle.
strings.season_turn.spring: The swallows are back under the eaves.
strings.season_turn.autumn: The grapes are in: the vintage begins.
strings.season_turn.nov: Cranes call high overhead, flying in a long V.
strings.season_turn.oct: The first rain. The whole land smells of dust and earth.
strings.season_turn.winter: The sea is closed. Ships are hauled up on the shore for the winter.

harbours.note: the triremes rest in their sheds at Zea and Mounychia
